a4252.speech: According to the police source, in general Christmas night passed “normally” and there was no disturbance of public order and tranquillity, that is, no arrests and no record of road accidents.

a4252.speaker: National Police of Cabo Verde (PN)
a4252.name: National Police of Cabo Verde (PN)
a4252.speech: Stressed that “Operation Christmas and New Year” is under way, having begun on 10 December and ending at the beginning of January 2025; the plan involves 162 officers from all six police stations on the streets day and night (Santa Catarina, São Salvador do Mundo, São Lourenço dos Órgãos, Santa Cruz, São Miguel and Tarrafal), with the aim of conveying a feeling of security to the population and reducing criminal incidents as far as possible during the festive season, covering public order, road traffic, safe commerce and the security of people and their property.

a4252.speaker: Health professionals at the Santa Rita Vieira Regional Hospital (HRSRV)
a4252.name: Health professionals at the Santa Rita Vieira Regional Hospital (HRSRV)
a4252.speech: Referred any information about Christmas night in the Emergency Department (BU) to the management of the hospital establishment.

a4252.speaker: Officials of the Santa Rita Vieira Regional Hospital (HRSRV)
a4252.name: Officials of the Santa Rita Vieira Regional Hospital (HRSRV)
a4252.speech: Up to the closing of the report, Inforpress had not managed to speak to them, as their offices were closed (no comment obtained).

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On her overall experience: “It has been a roller coaster but a very rewarding journey. The main satisfaction has been the recognition by Basotho of the strong and enduring friendship with the European Union and its 27 Member States and the impact the bloc has had in supporting the development of the country”; cited EU support for water and sanitation infrastructure, the Renoka programme, the NISSA database developed with UNICEF, the Equitable Lesotho programme, children courts and the inauguration of regional Ombudsman offices in Butha Buthe and Mohale’s Hoek.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On the lows: “The lows are related to unwarranted attacks against the EU and its intentions in Lesotho. When the EU was accused because of asking for accountability of funds provided to government and civil society organisations, I was very disappointed. We are bound to seek transparency in the management of resources by implementers in the interest of EU taxpayers and of final beneficiaries. We cannot tolerate mismanagement of funds. Equally I am disappointed by those who characterize EU partnership as a way to ‘encircle’ Lesotho and to control its natural resources. The EU has no hidden agenda.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On priorities and progress: “One word summarizes the achievements of the Lesotho-EU partnership: Access”; said the objective is to improve equitable access of people to water, sanitation, electricity, justice, education and health, noting Afrobarometer found Basotho perceived water as among the least accessible goods, and that in four years more Basotho have had access to basic services with the EU playing a major role.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On how her perception of Lesotho changed: said she arrived as Lesotho was emerging from the Covid-19 pandemic, that EU-funded programmes were impacted by the lockdown, that four years later all resources have been committed and delays caught up, but that initiatives such as the Energy Bill and actions to improve the business environment remain ‘work in progress’ and, if implemented, could have accelerated investments.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On the evolution of EU–Lesotho relations: described a strengthening of people-to-people relations, accompanying HM King Letsie III to the European Development Days in Brussels, the reception of Foreign Minister Lejone by High Representative Kaja Kallas, more frequent visits by EU Member State Ambassadors, and academic and journalistic exchanges: “Team Europe is not only a vague concept in Lesotho, It is a strong alliance aimed at creating value add for our communities.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On trade: said all exports of Lesotho to the twenty-seven EU member states are duty- and quota-free, the EU is committed to keeping markets open under the regional Economic Partnership Agreement, the trade balance already favours Lesotho because of diamond exports, and there is “no intention by the EU to ‘punish’ Lesotho for exporting successfully to our markets”; welcomed Lesotho’s visa waiver for EU citizens, calling Lesotho “a hidden gem, not yet discovered by international tourism.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On the national reforms process: “Let me be clear on that: the EU as such or I personally did not have then – and do not have now – a vision for the reforms. The EU came in support of the government of Lesotho only to fund the preparatory process of the constitutional reforms, in particular to allow the process to be as inclusive as possible”; said she is glad to leave when the 10th Amendment has been adopted by Parliament and the 11th is being prepared, and that the adoption of the reforms is a major milestone and their implementation a potential game changer, with the Inclusive Lesotho programme launched in May supporting civic education.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On ensuring funds are used effectively: said EU procedures set clear and transparent rules for tendering and procurement, partners are required to produce yearly audit and reporting over expenditure, and impact is followed through technical and steering committees, logical frameworks with clear indicators and targets, and close monitoring.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On lessons for future engagements: “Ownership and sustainability are the mantras of EU cooperation in Lesotho and elsewhere. The programmes are implemented by Basotho and for Basotho, according to national priorities”; said the EU threads lightly, localizes services, provides technical assistance only at government request, and stepped back after the preparatory phase of the reform process so as not to interfere with the parliamentary process.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On conditions for continued support: “Contrary to what is sometime assumed, there are no strings attached to the partnership with the EU: no imposition of legislative reforms, no controls imposed on national resources, no conditionality. The EU support takes predominantly the form of grants, hence not burdening the country with additional debt. The best way for Lesotho to guarantee future support is to implement successfully and transparently the available resources for the benefit of its citizens.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On priority sectors: said the bulk of EU resources during her mandate went to renewable energy and water and to the governance sector including social development, justice, electoral support and civil society participation, not counting support channeled via regional or global instruments such as humanitarian assistance or vaccinations.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On budget support: said that back in 2018 Lesotho was found falling short on the eligibility criteria for EU budget support given political uncertainty, slow macro-economic reforms and stagnation in development policy and Public Financial Management; noted the 2025 PEFA self-assessment published by the government provides a clear map of priority areas, and that the EU has continued supporting public financial management and oversight bodies.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On what must be achieved before budget support resumes: said Public Finance Management reforms, budget predictability and implementation are key, acknowledged efforts on domestic revenue mobilization, the adoption of the Procurement Act, improvements in arrears management and increased funds for the DCEO and other oversight bodies, and listed four conditions to be assessed positively (credible national strategies and reforms; stability-focused economic policies; a credible plan to improve public financial management and domestic revenue mobilisation; budget oversight and publicly available budget information), plus adherence to EU fundamental values of human rights, democracy and the rule of law; stressed that the absence of budget support has not affected the amount of resources provided but only the modality of their implementation.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On the programmes she is most proud of: said Lesotho invited the EU for the first time to deploy an election observation mission for the 2022 national elections, which produced a thorough report and recommendations in support of the Independent Electoral Commission, with a follow-up mission due in a few months: “It is not a process of finger-pointing, but a way to share experiences and create the better conditions for free and fair elections.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On where assistance could have been more impactful: said EU support to preparatory processes could have borne fruit earlier had the reforms been adopted sooner, that adoption of the water and energy bills now before Parliament would send a strong positive signal to financing institutions and investors, and that EU support to Basotho SMEs could have stronger impact with measures facilitating ease of doing business, international trade and foreign investment.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On EU funding of foreign judges: said the project came to its natural end in 2023 after two extensions and that once the funds were exhausted it was no longer possible to support the initiative, with the government since covering the continuation with its own resources.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On the most challenging and rewarding part of her ambassadorship: said it is equally challenging and rewarding to communicate about Lesotho to European institutions and Member States and about the EU in Lesotho, since mutual knowledge is limited and the twenty-seven member states rely greatly on the reporting, analysis and networking of the EU team.

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: Her message to Lesotho: said she made a point of highlighting the EU commitment to the poorest and most marginalized communities in all corners of the country, in line with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, citing civic registration of children, water and sanitation for 125 schools and 15 clinics, off-grid solar electricity in ten remote areas, and funding for film production and fashion designers: “I hope that such initiatives become catalysts for more growth and prosperity for all.”

a4422.speaker: Paola Amadei, European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.name: Paola Amadei
a4422.title: European Union Ambassador to Lesotho
a4422.speech: On her legacy and next posting: said the EU is a long-standing and reliable partner of Lesotho and that in 2026 the two will celebrate 50 years of relations; said she will return to EU Headquarters in Brussels to work on human rights and international justice ahead of her retirement next year, and hopes Basotho will welcome her successor, Ambassador-designate Mette Sunnergren.

a4549.speaker: Dr Buberwa Muchwampaka, National Coordinator for Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) Services, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a4549.name: Dr Buberwa Muchwampaka
a4549.title: National Coordinator for Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) Services, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a4549.speech: Said the country continues to make significant strides in its fight against HIV/AIDS. “Available data shows that Tanzania has performed exceptionally well in the fight against HIV/AIDS. The country is implementing comprehensive strategies to reach the global target of HIV viral suppression by 2030” ; cited ongoing interventions including community education to change attitudes and risky behaviours, condom promotion, male circumcision and comprehensive economic empowerment for people living with HIV as key pillars of the national response; said approximately 1.7 million Tanzanians are currently living with HIV, of whom 92 per cent are aware of their status, 98 per cent of those diagnosed are on antiretroviral therapy and 98 per cent of those on treatment have achieved viral suppression; noted that as of June 2024 over 7.4 million males across the country had voluntarily undergone medical circumcision, describing it as a remarkable milestone in HIV prevention.

a4549.speaker: Bwai Biseko, Assistant Regional Administrative Secretary (Human Resources and Management), Kagera Region
a4549.name: Bwai Biseko
a4549.title: Assistant Regional Administrative Secretary (Human Resources and Management), Kagera Region
a4549.speech: Commended the US government for its continued support through the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “On behalf of the government of Tanzania and people of Kagera Region, I extend our sincere gratitude to the US government. Their support has played a critical role in reducing HIV transmission in our communities” ; instructed eight councils in the region — Muleba, Bukoba DC, Biharamulo, Ngara, Karagwe, Kyerwa, Missenyi and Bukoba Municipality — to incorporate HIV and health delivery programmes in their 2025/26 financial year budgets.

a4549.speaker: Dr Emanuel Sarakikya, Kagera Regional Manager for Management and Development for Health (MDH)
a4549.name: Dr Emanuel Sarakikya
a4549.title: Kagera Regional Manager for Management and Development for Health (MDH)
a4549.speech: Confirmed that the two projects being handed over were the Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) programme and the DREAMS initiative; said that between 2016 and 2025 a total of 539,835 men and boys were circumcised in Kagera Region, representing 95 per cent performance against the set targets, and that approximately 35,918 adolescent girls and young women received support under DREAMS from 2022 to 2024. “The services provided under DREAMS include HIV screening, testing, counselling, community-based HIV, violence prevention and economic empowerment” ; revealed that 8,177 orphans and vulnerable children were supported under the initiative to improve their health, education and socio-economic outcomes, with support extending to their caregivers and families.

a4572.speaker: Abdel Fattah el-Sissi, Egyptian President
a4572.name: Abdel Fattah el-Sissi
a4572.title: Egyptian President
a4572.speech: Addressing the summit, el-Sissi said that the plan "preserves the right of Palestinian people in rebuilding their nation and guarantees their existence on their land."

a4572.speaker: Abdel Fattah el-Sissi, Egyptian President
a4572.name: Abdel Fattah el-Sissi
a4572.title: Egyptian President
a4572.speech: Speaking at the summit, el-Sissi said there is a need for a parallel path for peace to achieve a "comprehensive, just and lasting settlement" to the Palestinian cause. "There will be no true peace without the establishment of the Palestinian state," the Egyptian leader said. "It's time to adopt the launching of a serious and effective political path that leads to a permanent and lasting solution to the Palestinian cause according to the resolutions of international legitimacy."

a4572.speaker: Office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
a4572.name: Office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu

a4572.speaker: Ahmed Aboul Gheit, Arab League chief
a4572.name: Ahmed Aboul Gheit
a4572.title: Arab League chief
a4572.speech: Said the summit's final communique calls on the U.N. Security Council to deploy an international peacekeeping force in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. "Peace is the Arabs' strategic option," he told a news conference, adding that the communique rejected the transfer of Palestinians and endorsed Egypt's reconstruction plan. "The Egyptian plan creates a path for a new security and political context in Gaza," he said.

a4572.speaker: Final communique of the Cairo summit
a4572.name: Final communique of the Cairo summit
a4572.speech: Said Egypt will host an international conference in cooperation with the United Nations for Gaza's reconstruction, and a World Bank-overseen trust fund will be established to receive pledges to implement the early recovery and reconstruction plan.

a4572.speaker: 112-page draft of the Egyptian plan obtained by The Associated Press
a4572.name: 112-page draft of the Egyptian plan obtained by The Associated Press
a4572.speech: According to the draft, hundreds of thousands of temporary housing units would be set up for Gaza's population while reconstruction takes place; the rubble would be recycled, with some of it used as infill to expand land on Gaza's Mediterranean coast; in following years the plan envisages building "sustainable, green and walkable" housing and urban areas with renewable energy, and calls for the opening of an airport, a fishing port and a commercial port.

a4572.speaker: Israel
a4572.name: Israel
a4572.speech: Has embraced what it says is an alternative U.S. proposal for the ceasefire itself and the release of hostages; has warned of additional consequences; has ruled out any role for the Palestinian Authority in Gaza and, along with the United States, has demanded Hamas' disarmament; has vowed to maintain open-ended security control over both territories; says it killed over 17,000 militants, without providing evidence.

a4572.speaker: Human rights groups
a4572.name: Human rights groups
a4572.speech: Said that the suspension of aid violated Israel's obligations as an occupying power under international law.

a4572.speaker: Hamas
a4572.name: Hamas
a4572.speech: Has said it's willing to cede power in Gaza to other Palestinians, but won't give up its arms until there is a Palestinian state.

a4572.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
a4572.name: Donald Trump
a4572.title: U.S. President
a4572.speech: Suggested Gaza's roughly 2 million Palestinians be resettled in other countries. He said the United States would take ownership of the territory and redevelop it into a Middle Eastern "Riviera" ; has suggested Egypt and Jordan could take in large numbers of Palestinian refugees from Gaza.

a4572.speaker: Palestinians, Arab countries and human rights experts
a4572.name: Palestinians
a4572.title: Arab countries and human rights experts
a4572.speech: Roundly rejected the proposal, saying it would likely violate international law.

a4572.speaker: Riccardo Fabiani, North Africa director at the International Crisis Group
a4572.name: Riccardo Fabiani
a4572.title: North Africa director at the International Crisis Group
a4572.speech: Said Egypt was "trying to present a credible alternative focused on reconstruction and an indirect consultation mechanism for Hamas that could reassure Israel and the US."

a4572.speaker: King Abdullah II of Jordan
a4572.name: King Abdullah II of Jordan
a4572.speech: Meeting with Trump at the White House last month, offered to take in around 2,000 children for medical treatment.

a4572.speaker: Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis
a4572.name: Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis
a4572.speech: According to the hospital, the first group of around 30 children, accompanied by up to two family members, left Gaza for Jordan on Tuesday.

a4572.speaker: Jordan
a4572.name: Jordan
a4572.speech: Said the children are amputees and will return to Gaza when their treatment is complete.

a4572.speaker: Gaza's Health Ministry
a4572.name: Gaza's Health Ministry
a4572.speech: According to the ministry, Israel's 15-month offensive killed more than 48,000 Palestinians; it doesn't say how many were fighters, but the ministry says women and children made up more than half the dead.

a4590.speaker: Zimbabwe Football Association (statement)
a4590.name: Zimbabwe Football Association (statement)
a4590.speech: Said in a statement on Wednesday that President Emmerson Mnangagwa has pledged a winning bonus of US$150 000 per match for the players, technical staff, and support personnel ahead of the FIFA World Cup qualifiers against Benin and Nigeria.

a4590.speaker: Zimbabwean authorities
a4590.name: Zimbabwean authorities
a4590.speech: Have urged Zimbabweans to rally behind the national team, with fans encouraged to show their unwavering support, whether by attending games, watching from home, or backing the team on social media.

a4677.speaker: International Criminal Court (arrest warrants)
a4677.name: International Criminal Court (arrest warrants)
a4677.speech: Issued arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, on charges of crimes against humanity and war crimes, and also ordered the arrest of Hamas leader Mohammed Deif on the same charges.

a4677.speaker: Pentagon
a4677.name: Pentagon
a4677.speech: According to the Pentagon, some 10,000 North Korean soldiers have been moved to the Russian region of Kursk, near Ukraine.

a4677.speaker: Yoon Suk-yeol, President of South Korea
a4677.name: Yoon Suk-yeol
a4677.title: President of South Korea
a4677.speech: Declared martial law on 3 December on the justification that alleged pro-North Korean and anti-state forces were trying to destabilise the country.

a4677.speaker: Venâncio Mondlane, Mozambican presidential candidate
a4677.name: Venâncio Mondlane
a4677.title: Mozambican presidential candidate
a4677.speech: Contests the election results and called for protests, which have degenerated into violent clashes.

a4677.speaker: Vulnerable nations (at COP29)
a4677.name: Vulnerable nations (at COP29)
a4677.speech: Argued that the roughly $300 billion a year pledged by developed countries until 2035 was insufficient and that at least $500 billion a year would be needed to adequately confront the climate challenges.

a4677.speaker: Scientists
a4677.name: Scientists
a4677.speech: The intensity of the Valencia “cold drop” reinforces scientists’ warnings about the worsening of climate effects due to the warming of the Mediterranean.

a4915.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.name: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Spoke of Africa's “huge ambition not aligned with its reality,” urging leaders to pursue pragmatic, tested solutions to turn vision into action ; stated that Africa's demographic trajectory requires urgent economic re-configuration ; “This imbalance between supply and demand of jobs, compounded by a mismatch of skills, presents one of the continent's greatest risks,” the king warned ; called not simply for more jobs, but for a comprehensive ecosystem that leverages digital technology, to empower youth and women-led businesses, enabling SMEs to serve as engines of growth under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) ; announced plans to lobby traditional leaders and Heads of State to channel domestic funds into the Africa Investment Strategic Alliance (ASIA).

a4915.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.name: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Condemned coups in all forms and urged continental leaders to codify firm consequences for any regime that seizes power by force ; highlighted that “no matter how popular a coup might seem, it must face consequences rather than acceptance” ; cautioned that recent coups across Africa risk undermining democratic consolidation, stability and development ; cited the need for both the African Union and the United Nations to act decisively in ensuring that no military takeover receives international legitimacy; his message was unambiguous: coups are not simply a policy issue, but ‘a moral imperative’ demanding rejection ; proposed strengthening the PSC's role by codifying best practices from past interventions and creating a compliance mechanism under the AU General Assembly with binding timelines ; reiterated the call for fully operationalising the African Standby Force, enhancing financing through the AU Peace Fund, and forging innovative partnerships ; urged harmonisation of protocols with the United Nations Security Council, the European Union, Regional Economic Communities and the League of Arab States ; endorsed the Ezulwini Consensus, demanding permanent African representation on the UN Security Council; called attention to the fact that the denial of Africa's seat at the top table continues to weaken the continent's influence ; argued that this generation of African leaders must move “beyond rhetoric, with courage and unity,” to silence the guns.

a4915.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.name: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Emphasised that laws will be reformed and institutions strengthened to ensure effective monitoring, accountability and delivery of NDC 3.0 ; issued a clear call to international partners, multilateral agencies and the private sector to scale up predictable and sustainable climate finance; in his words, Eswatini is determined “to turn vulnerability into resilience,” but it cannot do so alone ; presenting Eswatini as a “net carbon sink,” reminded the world that the country's ecological footprint is already outweighed by its natural absorptive capacity.

a4915.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.name: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Framed the partnership with Google, Stardust and SHE Powers Africa as a bold step towards reimagining the country as an innovation hub, where youth are equipped with the skills to thrive in frontier industries such as biotechnology, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence ; stated that such initiatives should be seen as catalysts for the Sustainable Development Goals, with the potential to create jobs, improve livelihoods and strengthen service delivery.

a4915.speaker: International Monetary Fund
a4915.name: International Monetary Fund
a4915.speech: Projecting over 20 million young people joining the workforce annually by 2035, more than the rest of the world combined.

a4915.speaker: Mulualem Syoum, AeTrade CEO
a4915.name: Mulualem Syoum
a4915.title: AeTrade CEO
a4915.speech: Described the Alliance as “open to all those interested in inclusive growth.”

a4915.speaker: Ahunna Eziakonwa, UNDP
a4915.name: Ahunna Eziakonwa
a4915.title: UNDP
a4915.speech: Emphasised the resilience of African women and youth in the informal economy.

a4915.speaker: Mduduzi Matsebula, Minister of Health of Eswatini
a4915.name: Mduduzi Matsebula
a4915.title: Minister of Health of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Welcomed UNAIDS' announcement of a dramatic price cut for lenacapavir, a breakthrough long-acting HIV prevention drug, and described the reduction as ‘timely for Eswatini,’ given the country's persistently high rate of new infections among women of childbearing age ; confirmed the country would be among the first countries to roll out lenacapavir, with a pilot launch planned for World AIDS Day and wider distribution beginning in January 2026.

a4915.speaker: UNAIDS
a4915.name: UNAIDS
a4915.speech: Hailed the price reduction, from US$28,000 per patient annually to just US$40, as a ‘watershed moment’.

a4915.speaker: Eswatini Risk and Hazard (RH) analysis (report)
a4915.name: Eswatini Risk and Hazard (RH) analysis (report)
a4915.speech: The study paints a stark picture of the challenges ahead: without urgent action, droughts, floods, food insecurity and health crises are projected to intensify, with disproportionate effects on vulnerable groups such as rural communities, women, young people and persons with disabilities; the analysis highlights the agriculture, water and energy sectors as most at risk, demanding urgent interventions in climate-smart farming, renewable energy and integrated disaster financing.

a4915.speaker: Savannah Maziya, Minister of Information, Communication and Technology of Eswatini
a4915.name: Savannah Maziya
a4915.title: Minister of Information, Communication and Technology of Eswatini
a4915.speech: Declared that Emaswati youth could now realistically dream of one day travelling to space ; revealed that the MoU with Stardust includes plans to build capacity towards establishing a national space agency, with NASA involvement under discussion, putting emphasis on the fact that Eswatini should no longer be ‘a well-kept secret,’ but a continental leader in digital innovation.

a4948.speaker: Abdisalam Abdullahi Farah, Director of Aid Affairs for Galmudug's Ministry of Relief and Disaster Management
a4948.name: Abdisalam Abdullahi Farah
a4948.title: Director of Aid Affairs for Galmudug's Ministry of Relief and Disaster Management
a4948.speech: Emphasized the gravity of the challenge, stating that aid diversion is a major obstacle that directly impedes humanitarian efforts; highlighted that the program provides the necessary tools and techniques to effectively combat this issue.

a4948.speaker: Said Mohamed Adan, Humanitarian Coordinator for the Ministry of Relief and Disaster Management of the Southwest State
a4948.name: Said Mohamed Adan
a4948.title: Humanitarian Coordinator for the Ministry of Relief and Disaster Management of the Southwest State
a4948.speech: Noted that the partnership is a significant, progressive step forward; said it will greatly enhance the monitoring and investigation capabilities of humanitarian agencies throughout the country.

a4948.speaker: Prof. Mohamed Ahmed Mohamed Adalle, Assistant Commissioner of SoDMA for the Durable Solutions for IDPs Program
a4948.name: Prof. Mohamed Ahmed Mohamed Adalle
a4948.title: Assistant Commissioner of SoDMA for the Durable Solutions for IDPs Program
a4948.speech: Stated that the program is a vital pillar of SoDMA's broader strategy to ensure that humanitarian assistance is delivered directly to the people who need it most.

a5025.speaker: Gaza’s Health Ministry
a5025.name: Gaza’s Health Ministry
a5025.speech: Reported that in the past 24 hours alone at least 111 Palestinians were killed, including 91 civilians seeking humanitarian aid, and that 820 others were wounded in the same period, bringing the total number of casualties since October 7, 2023, to 60,249 killed and 147,089 injured ; “Many victims are still trapped under the rubble and on the roads as rescuers are unable to reach them.”

a5025.speaker: Gaza’s Health Ministry
a5025.name: Gaza’s Health Ministry
a5025.speech: Revealed that 18,592 children have been killed since the start of Israel’s offensive in October 2023; the ministry’s records show that nine babies were killed on the day of their birth, five on the first day, five on the second, and eight on the third, with additional figures including 88 children aged one month, 90 aged two months, and 78 aged three months.

a5025.speaker: Al Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, central Gaza
a5025.name: Al Aqsa Martyrs Hospital
a5025.title: central Gaza
a5025.speech: Has issued a dire warning, describing its situation as “catastrophic by all standards” ; hospital officials are calling for urgent intervention from international and humanitarian organisations to prevent further loss of life.

a5025.speaker: Wafa, Palestine’s news agency
a5025.name: Wafa
a5025.title: Palestine’s news agency
a5025.speech: According to Wafa, the hospital is overwhelmed by hundreds of wounded arriving amid ongoing attacks.

a5025.speaker: Rights groups B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel
a5025.name: Rights groups B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel
a5025.speech: Have accused Israel of committing genocide, citing the systematic destruction of Palestinian society and the deliberate dismantling of Gaza’s healthcare system.

a5025.speaker: International Criminal Court (ICC)
a5025.name: International Criminal Court (ICC)
a5025.speech: In November, issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity.

a5025.speaker: The White House
a5025.name: The White House
a5025.speech: Announced that US President Donald Trump’s Special Envoy Steve Witkoff will visit Gaza on Friday to inspect food distribution sites.

a5025.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House spokeswoman
a5025.name: Karoline Leavitt
a5025.title: White House spokeswoman
a5025.speech: “Tomorrow, Special Envoy Witkoff and Ambassador Huckabee will be travelling into Gaza to inspect the current distribution sites and secure a plan to deliver more food and meet with local Gazans to hear firsthand about this dire situation on the ground” ; added that Witkoff and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee had a “very productive” meeting with Prime Minister Netanyahu and other Israeli officials ; “The special envoy and the ambassador will brief the president immediately after their visit to approve a final plan for food and aid distribution in the region.”

a5025.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House spokeswoman
a5025.name: Karoline Leavitt
a5025.title: White House spokeswoman
a5025.speech: When asked about stalled negotiations with Hamas, said: “The quickest way to end the conflict is for Hamas to surrender, to release all of the hostages and to end this conflict. And that’s what the President wants to see. He’s made that very clear.”

a5025.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House spokeswoman
a5025.name: Karoline Leavitt
a5025.title: White House spokeswoman
a5025.speech: On the issue of Palestinian statehood, noted Trump’s opposition to recent moves by France, the UK, and Canada to recognise Palestine: “He feels as though that’s rewarding Hamas at a time where Hamas is the true impediment to a ceasefire and the release of all of the hostages.”

a5025.speaker: Israeli military (statement)
a5025.name: Israeli military (statement)
a5025.speech: Said Egypt, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates coordinated with Israel to drop 43 aid packages over Gaza, and that the packages containing food were dropped from planes to residents of southern and northern Gaza, again refuting “claims of deliberate starvation” in Gaza.

a5025.speaker: Medical sources in Gaza and the enclave’s authorities
a5025.name: Medical sources in Gaza and the enclave’s authorities
a5025.speech: According to them, at least three Palestinians starved to death in Gaza today.

a5025.speaker: The UN and other international aid organisations
a5025.name: The UN and other international aid organisations
a5025.speech: Have slammed the air drops as an ineffective and potentially dangerous move that fails to address the root cause of the mass starvation in the enclave, which is Israel’s blocking of necessities as a systematic policy.

a5131.speaker: Tendani Tsedu, spokesperson for the South African Medical Research Council
a5131.name: Tendani Tsedu
a5131.title: spokesperson for the South African Medical Research Council
a5131.speech: “Hand-on experience was the key principle that drove curriculum development, ensuring that every student that departs the CATIR facility is proficient in relevant technologies and skills that are high in demand across research, clinical and biotech industries, not just theoretical understanding” ; “In doing so, we hope that they will go on to contribute to science locally and abroad.”

a5131.speaker: Tendani Tsedu, spokesperson for the South African Medical Research Council
a5131.name: Tendani Tsedu
a5131.title: spokesperson for the South African Medical Research Council
a5131.speech: Said students who are trained in DNA sequencing technologies can apply those skills in forensic analysis, oncology testing, agriculture, wastewater monitoring and pandemic surveillance.

a5131.speaker: 2024 study by Labour Market Intelligence on graduate unemployment in South Africa
a5131.name: 2024 study by Labour Market Intelligence on graduate unemployment in South Africa
a5131.speech: According to the study, the unemployment rate across most tertiary study fields has steadily increased from 2015 to 2023, with graduates in administration, arts and social sciences, agriculture and science struggling to find jobs.

a5131.speaker: South African Journal of Human Resource Management (2024 study)
a5131.name: South African Journal of Human Resource Management (2024 study)
a5131.speech: Showed that in the science field there is a “potential gap between conventional academic education and the practical skills often required in professional environments”; it recommended educational institutions and science councils should act as hubs or incubators to address these problems: “By designing relevant curricula and creating job opportunities (such as internships), they can ensure graduates are more valuable to the labour market. Securing employment for South African unemployed graduates is challenging because of a lack of relevant work experience, limited information on effective job searches and low social capital.”

a5131.speaker: Marcin Kouri, Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.name: Marcin Kouri
a5131.title: Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.speech: “We want to equip them with the core skills in working in a laboratory, because working in a laboratory is not only operating the instrumentation, but understanding the processes in the lab, understanding how to manage a team, how to influence a team, how to manage finances [and] how to develop the laboratory to the next level.”

a5131.speaker: Marcin Kouri, Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.name: Marcin Kouri
a5131.title: Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.speech: “After Covid-19, we have learned a lot about the self-sustainability and sustainability of the African continent with vaccine manufacturing and pharmaceuticals, and we see many countries endeavouring to localise manufacturing in the different areas of the continent. South Africa is one of them” ; “We believe that the graduates will be a good talent to have in those new vaccine manufacturing sites or pharmaceutical-established new manufacturing entities” ; added that molecular science is a gateway into many other disciplines — research and development, healthcare, vaccine development, pharmacy or vaccine and pharmaceutical trials — so students have an opportunity to transfer their skills and pioneer new scientific innovations and solutions tailored for South Africa's needs.

a5131.speaker: Marcin Kouri, Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.name: Marcin Kouri
a5131.title: Thermo Fisher's senior director for Africa and the Middle East
a5131.speech: “The world is about entrepreneurship. Innovation is about putting ideas into execution and practice” ; “Imagine you are a student with an idea, but you have no way to access those instruments or facilities to try. Hopefully this centre will give that opportunity for innovators as well to come and join their ideas and potentially innovate in the country.”

a5344.speaker: Cynthia Rowe, FCDO Development Director
a5344.name: Cynthia Rowe
a5344.title: FCDO Development Director
a5344.speech: In her remarks, reaffirmed the UK's confidence in Jigawa's leadership: "We have a 20-year partnership with Jigawa State. Jigawa is really important. CRIBS provides a systematic approach to climate resilience, and we are keen to scale this across Jigawa and northern Nigeria."

a5344.speaker: Wafaa Saeed Abdellatef, UNICEF Country Representative
a5344.name: Wafaa Saeed Abdellatef
a5344.title: UNICEF Country Representative
a5344.speech: Described Jigawa as a model state in nutrition, sanitation, and climate resilience: "We are here to hand over upgraded, climate-resilient schools and health facilities funded by the UK government. Jigawa has become a model state, making a big difference in many areas. This is the first state in Nigeria to achieve and sustain Open Defecation-Free status and sustain that." ; also praised the state's "innovative Masaki initiative, which provides preventive and treatment services for malnourished children under five, and also the annual contribution of the state to match climate resilience funds that are critical in treating malnutrition."

a5344.speaker: Umar Namadi, Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.name: Umar Namadi
a5344.title: Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.speech: In his address, highlighted Jigawa's vulnerability to climate shocks, particularly perennial flooding: "Jigawa State has over the years been devastated by perennial floods with catastrophic damage to physical infrastructure, including roads, schools, and health facilities; loss of livelihoods; and most often, significant loss of lives. These also come with significant disruptions to smooth service delivery in the two key sectors of education and health, with direct negative impacts on the government's effort towards ensuring that children survive, grow, learn, and fulfill their potentials."

a5344.speaker: Umar Namadi, Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.name: Umar Namadi
a5344.title: Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.speech: Said that Phase I of the CRIBS programme successfully renovated about 90 health and education facilities across pilot local governments, including Chamo Primary School and Chamo Primary Health Centre, adding that for the first time in their history these facilities have now been remodeled to withstand the effects of climate change: "About a quarter of the projects, comprising eleven health facilities and eleven schools' infrastructure, are located across the three pilot Local Government Areas in Jigawa State. We hope to see a relatively higher coverage in the upcoming second phase of the program with more local governments and more facilities covered across the two sectors." ; reaffirmed his administration's resolve to expand CRIBS interventions across more local governments: "Let me use this opportunity to inform our partners - both the FCDO and UNICEF - that as a mark of our appreciation of these interventions and considering their long-term positive impacts, the Jigawa State Government will pursue a gradual scale-up of the CRIBS initiative. This is especially considering the risks and exposure of many parts of our state to climate change and the disaster continuously visited on health and educational infrastructure and facilities across many of the flood disaster-prone communities."

a5344.speaker: Umar Namadi, Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.name: Umar Namadi
a5344.title: Governor of Jigawa State
a5344.speech: Expressed deep appreciation to FCDO and UNICEF, describing them as Jigawa's most consistent and enduring development partners whose support has been critical to reforms in the delivery of basic services: "Even as technical and development assistance is waning in some quarters, FCDO and UNICEF have remained resolute and committed to supporting and collaborating with the Jigawa State Government. As we look forward to greater commitments in CRIBS and other programs being supported by the duo of FCDO the and UNICEF, we will remain ever-thankful to you."

a5357.speaker: Afrobarometer survey report, 'Amid growing food insecurity, Malawians favour alternatives to the Affordable Inputs Programme'
a5357.name: Afrobarometer survey report
a5357.title: 'Amid growing food insecurity, Malawians favour alternatives to the Affordable Inputs Programme'
a5357.speech: Findings show that a majority of Malawians think the Affordable Inputs Programme (AIP) is benefitting agro-related businesses or public officials more than intended farmers; 22 percent of the respondents think that poor farmers are the primary beneficiaries of the AIP. “Most [38 percent] think the programme mainly benefits businesses such as transporters, suppliers, importers, and agro-dealers while 16 percent think it is politicians, 13 percent government officials and eight percent traditional leaders.” ; 63 percent of the respondents are opposed to the abolishment of AIP with a majority supporting proposed alternatives such as providing input loans through farmers’ clubs or providing cash for inputs to poor farmers; support for loans through farmers’ clubs is popular in the Central Region, in urban areas and among respondents with moderate lived poverty.

a5357.speaker: Afrobarometer survey report
a5357.name: Afrobarometer survey report
a5357.speech: “These findings speak directly to the government and development partners, informing discussions on what might work to make subsidy programmes cost-effective in meeting the critical objective of food security.”

a5357.speaker: Sam Kawale, Minister of Agriculture (Malawi)
a5357.name: Sam Kawale
a5357.title: Minister of Agriculture (Malawi)
a5357.speech: Said yesterday that his ministry will keep on reforming the programme so that its efficiency and effectiveness are improved; said government is reforming the AIP to target households with land and labour while farmers without land are being moved to social cash transfer and public works programmes; on alternatives to AIP, said the National Economic Empowerment Fund is reaching out to farmers in clubs with input loans. “Our goal is to move people from subsistence farming to commercial farming by transitioning farmers from subsidy to loans and grants.”

a5357.speaker: Tamani Nkhono Mvula, agriculture policy expert
a5357.name: Tamani Nkhono Mvula
a5357.title: agriculture policy expert
a5357.speech: Said there have been cases when civil servants and other politically-connected people have been included as AIP beneficiaries; noted that smallholder farmers themselves sell the inputs to other people and this malpractice becomes difficult for the government to control. “One of the ways of reforming the AIP is to turn it into a loan programme as this will give farmers incentives to utilise the inputs.”

a5357.speaker: Leonard Chimwaza, agriculture expert
a5357.name: Leonard Chimwaza
a5357.title: agriculture expert
a5357.speech: Said the perception that AIP does not benefit the poor comes in due to artificial challenges that annually affect the programme such as late beneficiary selection, late procurement and distribution of the inputs and in some instances system failure.

a5357.speaker: World Bank
a5357.name: World Bank
a5357.speech: Said in August last year that AIP has done little to enhance food security, climate resilience, or productivity and has instead trapped many rural households in poverty by perpetuating a maize-based agricultural system.

a5424.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a5424.name: António Guterres
a5424.title: United Nations Secretary-General
a5424.speech: Noted at the recent UN Climate Ambition Summit that developed countries are not on track to meet their commitment to provide 100 billion dollars a year to support developing countries’ climate efforts.

a5424.speaker: Global Commission on Adaptation (research)
a5424.name: Global Commission on Adaptation (research)
a5424.speech: Research by the Global Commission on Adaptation shows that every dollar invested in resilience generates up to 10 dollars in net economic benefits.

a5503.speaker: Panel of successful entrepreneurs invited to the CIME
a5503.name: Panel of successful entrepreneurs invited to the CIME
a5503.speech: Each entrepreneur looked back on his own path and shared the experiences that had marked him.

a5503.speaker: Officials of the CIME (Centre for the Incubation of Micro-Enterprises)
a5503.name: Officials of the CIME (Centre for the Incubation of Micro-Enterprises)
a5503.speech: Expressed their sincere thanks to the companies invited for this day - the consulting and accounting firm HLB, GUEST AFRICA, INOCFAMS (Fishing and Maritime Services), the ARKIMED architecture firm, Hotel Horseed and the LE FOURNIL patisserie - for their presence and their contributions in terms of experience.

a5656.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.name: David Muwonge
a5656.title: spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.speech: Said that Elso Holdings currently manufactures 27 cleaning products at one production facility, distributes them through a single sales branch and employs thirty staff, of whom 21 are women and nine men.

a5656.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.name: David Muwonge
a5656.title: spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.speech: Said that employees are currently paid only part of their salary immediately, with the rest within a period of up to two weeks; he explained this unfortunate circumstance as being due to restrictions in the payout procedures.

a5656.speaker: Employees of Elso Holdings (complaints)
a5656.name: Employees of Elso Holdings (complaints)
a5656.speech: Complained of a lack of safety equipment and frequent work stoppages due to a lack of input materials.

a5656.speaker: An employee who wishes to remain anonymous
a5656.name: An employee who wishes to remain anonymous
a5656.speech: Reported that numerous workers were dismissed in November, before the factory moved from Prosperita to Lafrenz in Windhoek: “The problems began to become serious this year, but we have been struggling for two to three years already, for example in the area of overalls.”

a5656.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.name: David Muwonge
a5656.title: spokesperson for Elso Holdings
a5656.speech: Denies that there are unsafe working conditions; on the contrary, he insists that overalls as well as boots and aprons are always provided in all necessary situations: “The most dangerous product is not produced regularly, but only at the request of a particular customer. During the period of procuring the [raw materials necessary for the product] and manufacturing this product, it is ensured that both masks and gloves are worn. When hazardous chemicals are purchased, they are generally used directly and not stored, so that at no point are hazardous chemicals permanently stored.” ; However, he admitted that in May of this year an employee was injured on duty, although according to him this was the only workplace accident this year.

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On achievements: "We have a few achievements, first, we have embarked on a new project, where we advocate for the decriminalisation of abortion. We have a very big milestone in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries, where there is a committee that is formed to advocate for the decriminalisation of abortion. Lesotho is the chair of the committee through She-Hive Association because of our immense contribution in fighting GBV." ; "We also have the best practice of including women and girls through our project, where they become part of the decision makers in the communities. We are working with chiefs in this one, and I am proud to say that it is being implemented in five districts (Butha Buthe, Leribe, Berea, Maseru, and Mafeteng)." ; "Another achievement is that we have survived, because it is not easy to grow an NGO, and we are now 13 years old where other NGOs are formed and fail to succeed."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On impact and case statistics: "We have helped many victims, we have several cases which have been in the courts of law, and we have judgments, while some are still ongoing... I think we have about 15 cases so far that have been to court; others are cases that we solve without going to court." ; "We are now operating in seven districts, but we lack resources to reach the hard-to-reach districts due to lack of resources. We have formed task teams that are ready to tackle issues of GBV in Butha Buthe, Leribe, Berea, Maseru, and Mafeteng. We are yet to form similar teams in Mohale's Hoek and Quthing."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On male victims: "We have a programme that is called 'Men Engage' where we engage men to come and take the lead in the fight against GBV. Since it targets men, it encourages men to stop remaining silent when they are being verbally and emotionally abused." ; "Men become perpetrators because they are abused, they become angry because of emotional abuse, and then they keep their anger until it bursts, and they end up physically abusing their partners." ; "We have norms and culture that are harmful to our society, so we are trying to advocate for reviewing our cultural norms and traditions as Basotho... There is an English idiom that says, 'matters within the house are known to mice', but we are saying people should speak out because such silence has killed many women."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On community leaders: "We engage community leaders to give youths and women a platform to express their opinions on issues affecting them in their communities, and we have succeeded, as when there are public gatherings, they are given such opportunities."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On breaking the silence, bail and economic dependency: "We are advocating for a review of bail law, as to who is given bail. This is because a father can abuse his child, and the mother encourages the child to report the abuse, then the very same day, the father is granted bail. What is going to happen when he comes home?" ; "Often the man is granted bail and have a chance to murder her, hence we have these alarming statistics of women who are killed by men... in most cases, men are the providers, and that causes women not to report GBV. We encourage women to be economically independent and avoid dependency on their husbands."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On working with government: "We work closely with the Ministry of Social Development and Gender... We advocate for the review of laws and are assisting the government in reviewing laws where necessary. We are in partnership with the government to provide safe houses for the survivors of GBV."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On hard-to-reach communities: "We have not been able to access hard-to-reach communities like Thaba-Tseka, Mokhotlong, and Qacha's Nek, but we are planning to do that as long as we get funding. We are a bit challenged to reach them because of a lack of resources, but in the lowlands, we are already making a positive impact."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On the effect of the US aid cuts: "It negatively impacted us, especially that of President Trump, because he withdrew funding when we were about to start a programme aimed at supporting the victims of GBV, after we found a donor supported by USAID. A donor had asked us to give him the list of survivors for him to support economically. Immediately after we made the statistics, that is when the funding was withdrawn. It really affected us because we had engaged the survivors that they were going to be strengthened economically. It is tough as donors are now scarce because they used to get funding from the US. It is very difficult; we are struggling with operational costs, and we are even working with volunteers who are seeking to gain experience due to high unemployment."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On the organisation's hardest challenge: highlighted resource mobilisation as a major challenge that hinders them from reaching all the victims and survivors of GBV - "our biggest challenge has been resource mobilisation, as an organization that does great work, we don't have the money to be fully functional. It is because of our passion that this organization still exists... Some organizations get funding from the government, but we don't get it, yet they come to us for research and statistics."

a5741.speaker: Mamakhethe Phomane, She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.name: Mamakhethe Phomane
a5741.title: She-Hive Founder and Executive Director
a5741.speech: On the long-term vision: "We want to have a well-enhanced and strengthened coordination of services aimed at improving the lives of women and children who are survivors of domestic violence."

a5979.speaker: Dr Andy Gray, pharmaceutical sciences expert, senior lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and co-director of the WHO Collaborating Centre on Pharmaceutical Policy and Evidence Based Practice
a5979.name: Dr Andy Gray
a5979.title: pharmaceutical sciences expert, senior lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and co-director of the WHO Collaborating Centre on Pharmaceutical Policy and Evidence Based Practice
a5979.speech: In his latest #InsideTheBox column, explains how the system of medicine scheduling and prescribing authority works now and sets out how it might be improved ; argues that the corollary of making medicines prescription-only must be that those authorised to prescribe must be competent to do so, regardless of their professional registration; that the enabling provisions exist in South African law and are working; but that in the case of public sector nurses and clinical associates, the "back door" approach has been too easy, and expediency has won over principle.

a5979.speaker: Statistics South Africa, General Household Survey
a5979.name: Statistics South Africa
a5979.title: General Household Survey
a5979.speech: Every year, Statistics South Africa asks participants in the General Household Survey where they would first seek care if someone in their family is ill or injured. Two-thirds respond their first port of call would be a public sector clinic.

a5979.speaker: South Africa's National Drug Policy (1996)
a5979.name: South Africa's National Drug Policy (1996)
a5979.speech: One of the short policy statements in the document still informs current legislation and practice; it states simply: "At primary level, prescribing will be competency, not occupation, based."

a6012.speaker: Sofia Kassa (PhD), State Minister for Agriculture of Ethiopia
a6012.name: Sofia Kassa (PhD)
a6012.title: State Minister for Agriculture of Ethiopia
a6012.speech: Outlined plans to increase blended fertiliser production to 200,000 tns per year, covering 20pc of Ethiopia's fertiliser requirements.

a6036.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF and ROTARY (joint statement)
a6036.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6036.title: UNICEF and ROTARY (joint statement)
a6036.speech: "Today as the world commemorates World Polio Day, we, the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF and ROTARY, reaffirm our commitment to continue working with the Government of Ethiopia to ensure that Ethiopia stays polio free so we can maintain the success achieved in certification of the WHO African Region as free of wild poliovirus (WPV)" ; acknowledged that global eradication of wild poliovirus hasn't yet been achieved and hence the risk of importation and an ensuing outbreak remains a challenge, underscoring the need to remain vigilant and to strengthen routine immunization and disease surveillance in order to ensure Ethiopia and neighboring countries remain polio-free ; said the achievement was gained through the leadership of the Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health, commitment of frontline workers and generous support of polio partners such as WHO, UNICEF, ROTARY, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, USAID, CCRDA/CORE Group and other immunization partners ; called on the Government of Ethiopia and immunization partners to renew their commitment until polio is eradicated worldwide.

a6036.speaker: Africa Regional Certification Commission (ARCC) for Polio Eradication
a6036.name: Africa Regional Certification Commission (ARCC) for Polio Eradication
a6036.speech: On 25 August 2020, officially declared that the WHO African Region that constitutes 47 member states is free of wild poliovirus (WPV).

a6307.speaker: Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL) announcement
a6307.name: Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL) announcement
a6307.speech: Has announced a 25 basis point cut in its policy rate, bringing it down to 6.75 percent per annum, citing easing domestic inflation, improved reserves, and supportive regional monetary policy trends.

a6307.speaker: Dr Maluke Letete, CBL Governor
a6307.name: Dr Maluke Letete
a6307.title: CBL Governor
a6307.speech: Noted that the global economic outlook remains mixed, despite an upward revision in growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund (IMF): "While uncertainty persists due to trade disruptions and geopolitical risks, the IMF has revised its global growth forecast for 2025 upward to 3.0 percent, reflecting stronger-than-expected trade and fiscal support" ; he added that inflation trends remain uneven worldwide: "Advanced economies face cost pressures from housing, food, and fuel, while inflation is easing in some emerging markets."

a6307.speaker: Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL)
a6307.name: Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL)
a6307.speech: According to the CBL, Lesotho's economy has shown signs of modest recovery, driven by improved private consumption and resilient manufacturing, particularly textile exports to South Africa, in the first half of 2025 ; however, the CBL warned that the recovery remains fragile, with downside risks including weakening external demand, higher trade costs, and the withdrawal of donor-funded programmes such as the Millennium Challenge Compact II, and ongoing challenges in the mining sector were also highlighted.

a6307.speaker: Dr Maluke Letete, CBL Governor
a6307.name: Dr Maluke Letete
a6307.title: CBL Governor
a6307.speech: Reported that inflation in Lesotho eased to 4.3 percent in June 2025, largely due to lower global oil prices and a stronger Loti against the US Dollar. "Although inflation is expected to remain contained in the near term, risks remain from imported inflation, particularly from South Africa," he added.

a6307.speaker: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Central Bank of Lesotho
a6307.name: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Central Bank of Lesotho
a6307.speech: Resolved to raise the Net International Reserves (NIR) target floor from US$830 million to US$840 million, a move deemed sufficient to safeguard the loti-rand peg, and to lower the CBL policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.75 percent, aligning with both domestic conditions and the regional policy environment.

a6307.speaker: Dr Maluke Letete, CBL Governor
a6307.name: Dr Maluke Letete
a6307.title: CBL Governor
a6307.speech: Reaffirmed the bank's commitment to preserving the fixed exchange rate regime, stating: "The CBL will maintain adequate foreign exchange reserves to sustain the loti-rand parity and keep domestic inflation broadly aligned with South Africa's." ; "The Central Bank of Lesotho will continue to monitor domestic and external developments, including inflation trends, fiscal dynamics, SACU revenues, and South Africa's policy direction. The MPC stands ready to adjust the policy stance should risks to the peg or price stability intensify."

a6426.speaker: Brandon Hudspeth, US Embassy chargé d'affaires in Namibia
a6426.name: Brandon Hudspeth
a6426.title: US Embassy chargé d'affaires in Namibia
a6426.speech: Reaffirmed the US' longstanding support to Namibia through the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) ; Stressed the spirit of collaboration behind Namibia's success story: "I really do want to emphasise the term partnership because, yes, the US has provided assistance and technical advice, but it is really the Namibian partners, the health ministry, that have made this programme as successful as it has been. We have done PEPFAR in other countries, and they don't look like what they look like here in Namibia… and it's because of individuals like you." ; Reflecting on the visit: "It's been an excellent visit, especially in partnership with the health ministry. The most remarkable part was meeting patients directly and seeing how they've embraced this programming and are now helping deliver it to the next generation. That is what this has been about".

a6426.speaker: Dorothy Kabula, Zambezi governor
a6426.name: Dorothy Kabula
a6426.title: Zambezi governor
a6426.speech: Praised the US for its unwavering support: "This is very wonderful. We are doing very well in terms of our health situation in Namibia. The US has been with Namibia all along… We appreciate what the US has done so far. Keep on doing that. Do not remove these medicines. The partnership should carry on with Namibia."

a6426.speaker: Taimi Amaambo, deputy executive director at the Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6426.name: Taimi Amaambo
a6426.title: deputy executive director at the Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6426.speech: Echoed the importance of joint planning between Namibia and the US government: "What makes this partnership unique is that whenever we plan our programmes, it's a co-planning, co-organising activity. It's not like the US government says, 'This is what you need to implement.' Instead, it's a needs-based assessment we identify together. That is why we now see people who are coaches, living positively with HIV, and helping others to do the same." She added that the impact of this cooperation reaches far beyond health facilities.

a6495.speaker: Getachew Tessema, small-scale commercial farmer in Afar Regional State
a6495.name: Getachew Tessema
a6495.title: small-scale commercial farmer in Afar Regional State
a6495.speech: “I always had the vision to be a farmer” ; “What could be better than being self-sufficient? It’s just a matter of waiting for the right circumstances.”

a6495.speaker: Getachew Tessema, small-scale commercial farmer in Afar Regional State
a6495.name: Getachew Tessema
a6495.title: small-scale commercial farmer in Afar Regional State
a6495.speech: “It’s more profitable for us to add another round of harvest, but it will take more resources. The cattle which are normally banned from the farms during the regular cropping season come back. We’re expected to put up our fences for this season.”

a6495.speaker: Girma Tesema, 65, farmer in Dengugi Kebele, Lome Wereda
a6495.name: Girma Tesema
a6495.title: 65, farmer in Dengugi Kebele, Lome Wereda
a6495.speech: Said he and his fellow farmers have been pleading with local authorities to divert water from the Awash River — “They said it’s beyond their mandate” ; “We’re eager to begin” ; “We need pumps to bring the water to the surface.”

a6495.speaker: Local authorities (reported by farmer Girma Tesema)
a6495.name: Local authorities (reported by farmer Girma Tesema)
a6495.speech: “Said it’s beyond their mandate” to divert water from the Awash River as farmers had requested.

a6495.speaker: Arega Leta, 30, wheat farmer
a6495.name: Arega Leta
a6495.title: 30, wheat farmer
a6495.speech: “The soil isn’t suitable for farming wheat” ; argues the cluster farming arrangement has not been to his advantage.

a6495.speaker: Alemayeu Degefa, East Shewa Zone Agricultural Office expert
a6495.name: Alemayeu Degefa
a6495.title: East Shewa Zone Agricultural Office expert
a6495.speech: Disclosed that cluster farming in Lome Wereda began two years ago with 808 farmers in three kebeles who harvested a little over 37,000qtl of wheat in the first season, and that last year the initiative expanded to 3,100 farmers in eight kebeles who harvested nearly 349,000qtl of wheat.

a6495.speaker: Government counterparts (recently presented assessment)
a6495.name: Government counterparts (recently presented assessment)
a6495.speech: Reported that over 450,000hct of land had been irrigated in the past year, with the country’s wheat import yet to be made.

a6495.speaker: Zeleke Belay, irrigation engineering expert
a6495.name: Zeleke Belay
a6495.title: irrigation engineering expert
a6495.speech: “This financial commitment is important since it can get complicated finding support from donors in irrigation. Most water bodies cross borders and make for a hydro political issue.”

a6495.speaker: Data from the Agriculture Ministry
a6495.name: Data from the Agriculture Ministry
a6495.speech: Shows that the number of imported agricultural mechanization, irrigation and animal feed technologies and equipment has tripled since the removal of import duties.

a6495.speaker: Bereket Forsido, the Ministry of Agriculture’s director for agricultural mechanization
a6495.name: Bereket Forsido
a6495.title: the Ministry of Agriculture’s director for agricultural mechanization
a6495.speech: According to him, with high rates of migration and people leaving to cities looking for work this is no longer a labour-abundant sector, and mechanization is intended to step in to solve this; feed shortages for the oxen used in ploughing further complicate the problem.

a6495.speaker: Esayas Lemma, head of the crop development Directorate
a6495.name: Esayas Lemma
a6495.title: head of the crop development Directorate
a6495.speech: According to him, the strategy has taken into consideration several factors: the appropriate use of fertilizers, improved seeds, ploughing frequency, and weed control ; “The demand for wheat seeds was always known beforehand. This time, farmers were ready to produce and sell more seeds because they were informed that the demand would be there.”

a6495.speaker: Eshetu Habtewold, general manager of the Middle Awash Agriculture Development Enterprise
a6495.name: Eshetu Habtewold
a6495.title: general manager of the Middle Awash Agriculture Development Enterprise
a6495.speech: Told Fortune that in September the plan is to quadruple the size of the plot dedicated to wheat seed multiplication to 2,000hct ; “We used to grow cotton and then wait for about five months and then back to cotton. Now we are using the land continuously. We were selected because we have a well-established irrigation system and were prepared with the resources.”

a6495.speaker: Alemayehu Geda, professor of economics and researcher at Addis Abeba University
a6495.name: Alemayehu Geda
a6495.title: professor of economics and researcher at Addis Abeba University
a6495.speech: Says producing wheat domestically saves the average 1.7 billion dollars Ethiopia spends annually on cereal imports, which will go long in tipping the long-skewed scales of the country’s budget deficit: “This is equivalent to increasing the country’s export revenue by 50pc. It’ll ease the current forex crunch in the country” ; “Food supply is one of the major factors that contribute to the inflation in the country” ; “For a country with budget deficits for over 20 years, this can have a huge impact.”

a6495.speaker: Alemayehu Geda, professor of economics and researcher at Addis Abeba University
a6495.name: Alemayehu Geda
a6495.title: professor of economics and researcher at Addis Abeba University
a6495.speech: Remains hopeful about the “prospects of it [the initiative] becoming a reality” and urged the authorities to institutionalize the strategy “lest it lives and dies with those that hold power” ; “If this doesn’t tie in marketing value chains, it wouldn’t be the first-time overproduction has resulted in a fall in price for a commodity. Farmers might lose interest come next season.”

a6495.speaker: Adane Tuffa, assistant professor of economics at Addis Ababa University
a6495.name: Adane Tuffa
a6495.title: assistant professor of economics at Addis Ababa University
a6495.speech: Sees wheat as a commodity that can be used in many ways: “It can substitute for other grains in hard times. Other countries subsidize wheat to a great extent because they understand the strategic importance, despite being able to import. The work needed to make the country self-sufficient means that either farming will be intensified or more land will be farmed, creating more work for farmers” ; “Wheat can grow in different landscapes. This is not the case with teff, for instance, which is also difficult to farm with irrigation.”

a6495.speaker: Data from the Ethiopian Statistics Service
a6495.name: Data from the Ethiopian Statistics Service
a6495.speech: Shows that for almost a decade the land used for wheat farming averaged a little over 1.7 million hectares, and that this changed last year but only grew by 108,000hcts.

a6495.speaker: Federal officials
a6495.name: Federal officials
a6495.speech: Believe Ethiopia’s ambition to produce over 10.7 million tonnes (double the average over a decade) will give it an edge in the export market.

a6495.speaker: Shimelis Abdisa, chief of the Oromia Regional State
a6495.name: Shimelis Abdisa
a6495.title: chief of the Oromia Regional State
a6495.speech: “No doubt we will export wheat this year!” — tweeting back in September, he was upbeat about covering 1.7 million hectares of land with rainfed wheat farms and an additional one million hectares through summer irrigation.

a6495.speaker: Food & Agriculture Organization (FAO) periodical crop prospect report
a6495.name: Food & Agriculture Organization (FAO) periodical crop prospect report
a6495.speech: Reports Ethiopia as one of 33 countries in Africa which will need external assistance for food this year, and projects an estimated yield half of next year’s ambitious plans to scale up harvest.

a6495.speaker: UN-OCHA
a6495.name: UN-OCHA
a6495.speech: Warned that the number of people pushed to chronic food insecurity may reach 15 million this year, driven by soaring food prices, political instability and climate shocks.

a6495.speaker: US Department of Agriculture (quoted by Bloomberg)
a6495.name: US Department of Agriculture (quoted by Bloomberg)
a6495.speech: Called the plan a “very unrealistic and unachievable target” ; its Foreign Agricultural Services bureau forecasts Ethiopia’s production for the coming year at 5.5 million tonnes, half the volume the authorities look forward to seeing and one million tonnes short of the projections of the USAID-commissioned study.

a6495.speaker: Study commissioned by the USAID office in Ethiopia, “Crop Availability and Market Analysis for 2021/22”
a6495.name: Study commissioned by the USAID office in Ethiopia
a6495.title: “Crop Availability and Market Analysis for 2021/22”
a6495.speech: The study finds that not even in five years can Ethiopia exceed seven million tonnes, ploughing 2.1 million hectares of land; according to the study, authorities may have a fallback plan in the 600,000tns of wheat they have budgeted to import through the World Food Programme (WFP), double the volume imported last year.

a6509.speaker: NGO Regulatory Authority (NGORA)
a6509.name: NGO Regulatory Authority (NGORA)
a6509.speech: In a stark revelation, has exposed the alarming truth behind the operations of many Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) in Malawi—funds meant for community development are being siphoned off through excessive allowances, fuel expenses, and travel costs.

a6509.speaker: Edward Chileka Banda, CEO of NGORA
a6509.name: Edward Chileka Banda
a6509.title: CEO of NGORA
a6509.speech: Said NGOs in Malawi are spending a disproportionate amount of the funds they mobilize on non-essential costs, leaving only a fraction for the very communities they claim to serve: “There is a culture where NGOs spend more money on allowances, travel, and fuel than on actual projects that benefit the poor. In some cases, 90% of the mobilized funds are spent on these overhead costs, and a paltry 10% is what trickles down to the community.” ; “For example, people are traveling to Mulanje spending K10 million on allowances while only K500,000 goes to support the community. This doesn't make sense. This is the kind of resource capture that must stop.” ; “We cannot talk about development if this culture of allowances continues. We must change the way NGOs operate to ensure that more money reaches the people who need it.”

a6509.speaker: Edward Chileka Banda, CEO of NGORA
a6509.name: Edward Chileka Banda
a6509.title: CEO of NGORA
a6509.speech: Stressed that the localisation agenda now being heavily discussed is the perfect opportunity to reassess and realign the way NGOs operate in Malawi, and noted that a systemic overhaul is necessary to ensure that foreign aid and NGO resources are used effectively and responsibly.

a6509.speaker: Bernadetta Mkonyola, representing the UN's Resident Coordinator in Malawi
a6509.name: Bernadetta Mkonyola
a6509.title: representing the UN's Resident Coordinator in Malawi
a6509.speech: Highlighted the importance of localization, emphasising that empowering local communities, particularly women, youth, and the elderly, is the key to driving true development: “Localization is not just about trickling down money; it's about giving power to communities to sit at the table with decision-makers. Only through consultation with those on the ground can we ensure that development agendas are relevant and sustainable.”

a6558.speaker: Rune Skinnebach, outgoing EU Ambassador to Malawi (Daily Nation interview)
a6558.name: Rune Skinnebach
